Jorge Luis Borges imagined a garden where every possible outcome of every possible decision branches endlessly into parallel realities. Richard McElreath, in his excellent book "Statistical Rethinking", borrowed the image to make a point about statistics: don't try to be clever in the face of uncertainty; be thorough. To be thorough, one has to count all the ways the world could have produced what is being observed, and let the count inform the conclusion. Simple, and yet surprisingly hard to remember when staring at a machine learning model that, by all reported metrics, seems to be working well enough to warrant a publication.


## An Underdetermined Problem
The ocean surface reflects light in ways that carry, somewhere in their spectral shape, a whisper of what's living beneath. Diatoms, dinoflagellates, coccolithophores — each community leaves a faint optical fingerprint, and the dream of ocean color remote sensing is to read that fingerprint from space and reconstruct who's home. It's a lovely idea. It's also, in the technical sense, an underdetermined problem: the same spectrum can be produced by multiple different community configurations, for reasons that are not noise but physics. Photoacclimation means the same species presents differently depending on its light history. The pigment packaging effect means cell size bends the absorption signal in ways that are independent of who's there. Dissolved organics and sediments pile their own signatures on top. The garden, in other words, has a lot of forks.

## The Pruned Garden
Training a machine learning model on real ocean observations would be the natural response — but real coincident measurements of ocean spectra and community composition are scarce, expensive, and sparse in space and time. The practical workaround is to train on simulated data instead: a coupled physical and biogeochemical model of the ocean that generates both spectra and community compositions in the millions. It sounds reasonable. The trouble is that the simulation, necessarily, makes simplifying choices. It assigns each phytoplankton group a fixed optical identity, represents the messy continuous process of photoacclimation with a handful of discrete states, and operates mostly in the open ocean, away from the murky coastal waters where dissolved organics and sediments complicate everything. The result is a garden with most of the forks pruned away — a tidy, well-lit path from spectrum to community composition that the model learns to walk confidently. And there are your impressive performance metrics. But what the model has learned, at least in part, is how to invert the simulation's own rules, and taking it into the real ocean — where the forks are back and the path is genuinely ambiguous — that confidence becomes a liability rather than an asset.

## Don't be Clever
This is where McElreath's injunction bites. Don't be clever. Don't pick a path and commit. Count all the ways the data could have been produced and let the distribution speak. That counting procedure, applied rigorously, is Bayes' theorem — not as one framework among many but as the uniquely correct way to update beliefs when the world is ambiguous. And the real ocean is ambiguous in ways that more simulations, or more finely tuned machine learning, won't resolve. The ambiguity is not ignorance waiting to be cured by larger datasets. Some of it is irreducible. A model that produces a point estimate — this community, this confidence — has no way to say "actually, three other communities are about equally consistent with this spectrum." A posterior distribution does.

## Difficult, Difficult, Lemon-Difficult
There is a practical sting in this. Specifying the likelihood — the forward model from community to spectrum — with enough fidelity that the posterior is meaningful is genuinely hard. Get the likelihood wrong and you get a posterior that is confidently wrong, which is worse than a frequentist shrug. But this is a solvable engineering problem, and more importantly it is an honest one: Bayesian model criticism gives you the tools to check whether your likelihood is adequate, and to say so explicitly when it isn't.

## The Heavy Burden of the Prior
The deeper point is this. In a problem where the data are sparse, the physics are ambiguous, and the prior — what communities are ecologically plausible in a given place and season — is scientifically meaningful, the prior is load-bearing. Pretending otherwise, which is what a purely data-driven approach does, is not neutrality. It is an unexamined assumption wearing the costume of objectivity. Bayes at least makes you write your assumptions down.
Borges' garden was a metaphor for time and fate. McElreath's was a metaphor for probability. In ocean color remote sensing, it turns out to be a pretty accurate description of the forward problem. The phytoplankton don't care how many forks you'd prefer there to be.

## A Garden Among Gardens

The garden McElreath [-@mcelreath2020] describes — and the one I attempt to draw earlier in this post — is nature's garden: all the ways the ocean could have produced the spectrum I observed. Every fork in the tree is a physical or biological ambiguity that exists whether or not anyone is measuring it. This is the garden I can at least attempt to draw.

But nature's garden is not the only one in play. A second garden sits inside the first: the simulation. When a coupled physical-biogeochemical model is used to generate training data, it makes choices — fixed optical properties per phytoplankton group, a handful of discrete photoacclimation states, an open ocean domain that excludes the messy coastal waters where biology gets complicated. These choices prune the forks. The simulation is not wrong, exactly — it represents real physics — but it represents a narrow, tidy slice of it. It is nature's garden with most of the branches cut away. A model trained on it learns that tidy slice as if it were the whole garden.

And then there is a third garden, orthogonal to the first two. This is the researcher's garden: the space of analytical decisions made before and after the model is built. Which simulation to trust. How to split training and test data. Which hyperparameters to tune. Which performance metrics to report and which to quietly set aside. This garden is not physical — it does not exist in the ocean. It exists in the decisions, some conscious and some not, that determine what the model ever sees and how its performance is judged. Gelman and Loken [-@gelman2013garden] identified this garden in a different context — the replication crisis in psychology — but it grows just as readily in ocean remote sensing. A model that achieves an R² of 0.95 on held-out simulated data has found one path through this garden. Whether that path leads anywhere real depends on the first two.

The three gardens are not nested in any simple way. The simulation garden is a subset of nature's garden — same kind of thing, just smaller. But the researcher's garden is a different kind of thing entirely: epistemological rather than physical, a space of choices rather than phenomena. What connects them is interaction. The researcher's choices determine which slice of nature's garden the simulation represents. The simulation's choices determine what the model learns. And the model's reported performance is the leaf at the end of one particular path through all three gardens simultaneously.

The figure earlier in this post draws only the first garden. The dashed circles acknowledge that even there, I am showing samples from a continuum rather than the continuum itself. The second garden is implied by what the figure leaves out. The third garden is the hardest to draw — not because it is more complex, but because it requires the researcher to turn the lens on themselves. The phytoplankton don't care how many gardens you'd prefer there to be.
